title: How Dan Osborn Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns show a different path for Democrats in deep-red states. In places where the party label struggles, an independent with local credibility may perform better than a standard Democratic nominee.
author: gamerdoglover

image.alt: Dan Osborn beside the U.S. Capitol and a Proud Union Home sign

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.

Nebraska is not considered in any pathway to victory for Democrats in 2026 when it comes to the Senate. This is in large part because Republicans dominate the state. Democrats struggle in deep-red Nebraska due to negative brand recognition. AP reported that Nebraska Democrats in 2026 are looking for others who can "outperform the Democratic label."

Osborn is in a different form. He ran as an independent in 2024 and is running again in 2026. He leans on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. He campaigns on workers' rights, wages, corporate power, and taking money out of politics.

We saw what happened in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but the race was shockingly close historically in Nebraska. Fischer won by only about six points, while in 2024, the state voted for Donald Trump by over 20 points. What we learned was simple. Some voters who might reject national Democrats would still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economics.

On May 12th, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in Nebraska. She campaigned simply on withdrawing and supporting Osborn. This reduces a split anti-Ricketts vote and avoids a three-way race, which all but guarantees Republicans hold on in the state.

Nebraska Democrats appeared to understand that when Nebraska's race focuses on the national aspect, Ricketts wins. When it goes local, Osborn stands to benefit. This is what Democrats need to study. Sometimes in a deep-red state, stepping aside is more strategic.

Of course, this does not work anywhere. You need someone with local credibility and a message voters believe. In a state where voters have histories of ticket splitting or independents, it might be the right move. However, national Democrats must stay disciplined. If these independents are turned into Republican versus not Republican, the brand is weakened.

Even if what the forecast model says holds, and Osborn loses, the current projected margin of only 3.9 points at the time of writing for Republicans shares a big message. Democrats must reinvent their strategies in the deep red or become a figment of the past for those living in red states.
The takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats need more flexibility. Sometimes the best Democratic move is to support a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.

There are much more of Dan Osborn. In Montana, Seth Bodnar is staging an independent run against Kurt Alme after the incumbent dropped out last moment. However, due to party rules, the Montana Democratic Party has failed to withdraw their candidate and or endorse Seth Bodnar. Even then, this is being somewhat replicated across state legislatures in the deep red. Regardless, as previously discussed in this article, Democrats may have an issue if they go all-in with this strategy.

Alaska is an interesting example of local Democratic control in the deep red state. Well, it doesn't relate to what is being discussed, it does show the potential cross-appeal in a state like Alaska which votes red in most national races though is competitive for the 2026 Senate. Democrats are in a governing coalition alongside a fringe group of Republican moderates in the State legislature and have frequently clashed with the Republican governor over how to spend the budget. Alaska shows how even in the deep red, localization, like candidates of Dan Osborn, can work out for Democrats. Localization of these legislative issues, along with handling of state elections, has enabled Democrats to maintain this governing majority alongside the moderate Republicans.

Moving into November, Nebraska will either become more competitive or seek to have Dan Osborn lose again. Regardless, this new strategy has proven to be a large hit-or miss for Democrats, but the results speak for themselves. And will speak loud again in 2026.

title: Clash of Cash: The Spectacle We Call the California Governor's Race
dek: After a year of speculation and controversy, the California Governor's race is coming to an end, and it's leaving with a bang.
author: Nathan Wang

image.alt: Tom Steyer and Xavier Becerra besides a McDonald's sign, a Chevron oil barrel, and a stack of cash.

content.text: The California Governor's race is almost over, but it's not dying down quite yet.

With the Democratic frontrunner Eric Swalwell dropping out and resigning from Congress in disgrace, the possibility of Democrats being locked out of the general election, and the new insurgent frontrunner being a former Biden admin official, what more could you ask from this exciting race to be at the forefront of the 4th largest economy in the world? Well, this race is coming to an end, but who will win in November, or even make it through the primary, is still very unbeknownst to us."

The new leader in this race is Xavier Becerra, who has placed first in the three latest polls from Emerson College, Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, and the Public Policy Institute of California, is clearly in the driver's seat. However, depending on who makes it with him to November, determines if this race will continue to be a grueling divide within the Democratic party, or Becerra's odds to be the next Governor of California will be sealed.

In the three previously mentioned polls, Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton places second place in two out of the three, which means he takes the second slot of advancing to the general election in November, taking on Xavier Becerra. However, Tom Steyer, with the millions of dollars of his own money he has funneled into ad spending, is still a formidable threat to both Hilton and Becerra's odds. He statistically tied with Hilton in the Emerson College poll, placing less than 1% ahead of Hilton when leaners were pushed.

Steyer's threat to Becerra in the November election cannot be spoken enough. Most polling shows Steyer crushing Becerra among Republican voters, which would be a deciding factor in the November election. However, Becerra still captures a sizeable lead above Steyer among registered Democratic and independent voters. What this really means is that June 2nd could very well decide the next Governor of California; it all depends on who gets second place.

Other than political affiliation, Becerra places the most strongly among Hispanic and female voters; he is also the most favorable in the 45-54 age group. Steyer does the best among black and young voters.

What about the other candidates in this race, you might ask? Well, besides the top three, all others have seen dips in polling or losses of momentum. The other main Republican candidate, Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, has died off in polling ever since Trump's endorsement consolidated the Republican vote around Steve Hilton.

At one point, the frontrunner, former U.S. Representative Katie Porter, has also failed to take up a lane in the crowded field of candidates; sometimes she polls as low as 4 or 5 percentage points. Porter's base still remains mainly younger progressive voters, so in a Steyer-Becerra general election, you can expect her base to skew heavily to the former.

Other Democrats in the field, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan and former Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, also failed to ever break double digits in polling, even though Mahan had big cash, his priorities and platform never broke through with voters. During the rise of Becerra, the former Los Angeles Mayor also saw a tick in support, though most of it has since consolidated around Becerra.
In a Steyer-Becerra general, you can expect Mahan's unpredictable base of voters to split either way and Villaraigosa's Hispanic base in southern California to skew heavily towards Xavier Becerra.

With all said and done, the California Governor's race has been one of the most mind-boggling races this decade has seen so far, and it could stretch on for another 5 months. We can only wait and see, especially with the treacherous time that takes the Golden State to count its votes.

Does Becerra meet expectations and place first? Will Steyer's massive pile of cash break through to get him to second place? Can Republicans actually be locked out of the November general? All of these answers will be answered on Tuesday.
